name: Designer descriptions (Google DESCRIPTION.en_us.html, Fontshare `story`, indie foundry pages), condensed offline by an LLM into short 'looks like' notes
what_it_is: Google: one HTML description per family folder in google/fonts, 1,754 files (ofl 1,705, apache 44, ufl 5; the claim is confirmed), median 63 words (mean 83, 10th percentile 31, 90th 164, max 482), 928,155 characters in all, about 232k tokens. Fontshare: a `story` text per family in the api.fontshare.com/v2/fonts response the app already calls; all 64 catalog Fontshare families have one, median 198 words (min 16, max 410), 77,052 characters (~19k tokens). Indie: nothing usable in the app's data. Use & Modify pages (191 cached HTML files) hold only a family list, licence, keywords and font links, no prose; the Collletttivo builder says GitHub has no descriptions for its repos; Velvetyne descriptions are short GitLab repository descriptions (not cached; I did not request them); Tunera has a site page per family that I did not read [uncertain]. The proposed product is a one-line 'looks like' note per family, written once by an LLM from the text, with a quoted evidence span.
provider_and_url: Google: the authors' and Google's texts in https://github.com/google/fonts (ofl|apache|ufl/<family>/DESCRIPTION.en_us.html; the README confirms one per family folder). Fontshare / Indian Type Foundry: https://api.fontshare.com/v2/fonts (field `story`), pages https://www.fontshare.com/fonts/<slug>. Indie: usemodify.com (keywords only), github.com/collletttivo, tunera.xyz, GitLab for Velvetyne; never velvetyne.fr.
catalog_coverage: Measured by me (SCRATCH/gf matched by slug of the family name; catalog rebuilt from remote-v7.json + server/data/*.json). Google source: 1,443 of 1,760 rows (82.0%) have a description: 1,442 of the 1,644 true Google families (87.7%), plus 1 non-Google Fontsource row that shares a name. The 317 Google-source rows without one are 115 non-Google Fontsource families plus 202 real Google families, mostly new ones (Bitcount x12, BBH x6, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, Alan Sans...) and some sub-family names whose text may sit in a sibling folder (not checked). Fontshare 64 of 64 (100%). Velvetyne 0/63, Collletttivo 0/26, Tunera 0/23, Use & Modify 0/163 (no prose in the app's data). Total with prose: 1,507 of 2,099 rows (71.8%); 592 have none (275 indie + 317 Google-source). Overlap with the thin-tag rows: of the 345 rows with one tag or none, 175 (51%) have a Google description and 170 do not (97 of them are non-Google Fontsource families); of the 567 rows with two tags or fewer, 326 have prose (a Google description or a Fontshare story) and 241 do not.
granularity: Per family folder. Sub-families share or repeat text: ten Big Shoulders families carry the same paragraph, and Saira's text starts 'This is the Normal family, which is part of the superfamily'. Nothing per style, weight or italic.
signal_type: Semantic mood and overall look in the designer's own words, mixed with history, designer bios, language support and version notes.
mood_dimensions_covered: Counts are descriptions (1,754) after I stripped contribution links and version boilerplate, measured by me with keyword patterns; Fontshare stories are 64. MOTION/ACTIVE (rare, but precise when present): speed 5, fast 4, motion 2, velocity 1, momentum 1, racing 1 (13 distinct families); 7 are genuine: Faster One ('an impression of velocity'), Dynalight ('dynamic high speed script'), Smooch ('speedy personality'), Hurricane ('fast moving spirited brush script'), Rouge Script and Euphoria Script ('fast curves'), RocknRoll One ('momentum', 'dynamic feel'). Reggae One ('rhythm, movement and energy') and Fugaz One ('a very dynamic font') only turn up under the looser words below. The rest are noise ('fast page loading' in Vesper Libre, 'motion graphics' in Poiret One, 'speedier penned styles' in Uncial Antiqua). Looser words add more noise: 'action' 18 (10 are the Big Shoulders sub-families: 'political action'), 'movement' 18 (mostly handwriting movement, one is Rapid Eye Movement), 'dynamic' 24 (including 'dynamic flexibility'), 'energy' 10, 'sporty/athletic' 19 (Jersey x8 knitting fonts, Alumni Sans Collegiate One, Playball, Tourney, Goldman), 'lively' 17. Fontshare stories: energy/dynamic/motion/speed/movement/rhythm 6 of 64. FUTURISTIC/TECH: 74 mention futuristic, sci-fi, spaceship, technological or technical (explicit futuristic/sci-fi/spaceship: 15 families). This fills Google's tag gap for Exo ('tries to convey a technological/futuristic feeling'), Exo 2 (no Futuristic/Techno tag at all), Oxanium ('feels at home on the head-up display of a spaceship'), Rajdhani ('technical or even futuristic'), Contrail One ('jet age', slight slant), Tourney, Goldman. It does not help Saira ('a sans serif system'), Teko (script support) or Racing Sans One (a history of 1800s sans); Bungee and Climate Crisis have no description at all. ELEGANT/REFINED 104, CALM/GENTLE/SOFT 87, HANDMADE/BRUSH/PEN 210, PLAYFUL/FUN/FRIENDLY 163, BOLD/HEAVY/PUNCHY 191, RETRO/VINTAGE 30. Shape words: slant/italic 179, condensed/narrow 130, geometric 91, rounded 79. 86 descriptions name a famous font as a reference (Eurostile, Microgramma, Garamond...), which gives the model a similarity anchor. Visual vocabulary overall: 1,432 of 1,754 (82%) contain at least one look word (contrast, stroke, curve, slant, serif, geometric...), 322 (18%) contain none; 1,108 (63%) contain a feel word.
query_style_specificity: Plain keyword search is poor for both kinds: 'fast', 'speed' or 'motion' finds 13 families with 7 genuine, and words like 'friendly' or 'playful' hit 163 descriptions with no ranking. Where it shines is as evidence the model reads for a shortlist: tight genre requests ('futuristic', 'sporty', 'jet age', 'headlines for action films') because designers state intent in plain words. Loose mood requests are served better by the tags (Happy, Cute, Calm). For motion, descriptions catch fonts the tags miss (Smooch, Hurricane, Reggae One, Rowdies, Tourney, Goldman) and the tags catch fonts the text never mentions (Faster One aside, Climate Crisis, Bungee, Racing Sans One).
quality_evidence: Offline reading by me, no LLM run yet. I read the keyword-in-context lines for speed, fast, motion, velocity, momentum, racing, energy, movement, action, dynamic and sport across all 1,754 texts and the descriptions of 23 tag-gap and motion fonts. Findings: (1) text and tags are complementary: in my 17-font motion oracle (families whose text says speed, fast curves, momentum, action or sport) Google's Active at 40+ finds 8, Active or Excited 9, adding Futuristic or Techno 12; text alone finds all 17 by construction, so this oracle favours text and I do not read it as a fair score. (2) For futuristic, text and tags agree on 12 of 15 (the three misses are Exo, Exo 2, Azeret Mono, where the text is right and the tags are silent). (3) About 18% of descriptions have no look word, so a condensed note would be empty for them. No published evaluation of descriptions for font search was found; an LLM-written note must be judged by the evaluation_hook below.
known_noise: Boilerplate and non-look content: 'To contribute, see github.com...' lines, 'Updated September 2015: Internal metadata corrected', language-support paragraphs, designer bios; after stripping boilerplate, 36 descriptions have fewer than 10 words and 96 fewer than 20; 322 (18%) have no look word. Shared paragraphs across sub-families (Big Shoulders x10). Literal keyword hits are about half noise (examples above). Some descriptions describe a sibling or the project, not the look (Saira: 'This is the Normal family'). Pre-2016 texts carry marketing flourish ('ready for action' in Rochester is a figure of speech for an elegant script, not motion). An LLM condenser can also hallucinate a look the text never states; a required quoted span that I can string-match against the source avoids that.
name_and_memory_bias: The text itself reduces name bias (Oxanium's 'head-up display of a spaceship' needs no name), but an LLM writing the notes knows the fonts and may fill gaps from memory; instruct it to use only the text and give it the description with the family name removed (key rows by id). Descriptions also repeat the name's own story (Racing Sans One's text never says fast; only the name does), so name-driven matches survive. Mentions of famous fonts (86) are a memory anchor on purpose.
untagged_rows: Covers 1,507 of 2,099 rows; 592 get nothing (all 275 indie rows, 115 non-Google Fontsource, 202 real Google families) and would be silently ranked only on their tags if notes become the main signal. It helps the thin-tag rows only partly: 175 of the 345 rows with one tag or none, and 326 of 567 with two or fewer. For the indie gap it does nothing. The notes should be added only where they exist and never penalise a row that has none.
text_interference_risk: Not applicable: no rendered text; the input is the designer's prose.
integration_path: A precomputed data file, server/data/looks.json, one entry per family, produced once by a batch script and committed: {"Smooch": {"looks":"brushy handwritten script, slightly bolder, speedy","evidence":"full of speedy personality","motion":2,"tech":0,"src":"gf","hash":"<sha1 of source text>"}}. The batch script reads SCRATCH/gf (or a refresh from google/fonts) and Fontshare `story`, calls Haiku through `claude -p` (same pattern as server/vibe.ts askClaudeCode, JSON schema, no tools) in batches of about 25 families, and refuses any note whose `evidence` string is not found in the source text. Prompt use: in compactCatalog add `| looks: <note>` only for rows with fewer than 3 tags or no mood tag (about 570 rows), or only for the shortlist after a code-side filter. The same file also gives a free lexical boost: motion/tech scores (0-3) become weights in a pre-LLM scoring step (the search-design item), with the quoted evidence as the explanation. Merge key: family name with the same slug rule as server/catalog.ts; `hash` lets reruns touch only changed or new rows.
tokens_per_row: A note is about 20-30 tokens. For all 1,507 rows with prose: about +38k tokens (catalog 41k -> ~79k, the 'Lost in the Middle' risk grows). For only the thin rows (~570): about +14k. As shortlist-only evidence (60-80 rows): about 2k per search. Static between searches, so cacheable.
vocabulary_alignment: Adds new free-text terms in the designer's own words (jet age, head-up display, brushy, speedy) instead of mapping onto Google's tags. To align, the batch step can also emit scores for a fixed handful of Google tags (motion 0-3, tech 0-3), which would let one vocabulary cover Google, Fontshare and any new family with prose.
explainability: Strongest of the text-based options: a result can quote the designer, e.g. Dynalight: 'a dynamic high speed script inspired by a vintage luggage tag for the Southern Pacific 4449 Daylight steam locomotive'.
determinism: The notes are generated once and stored, so the same request sees the same notes; selection by Haiku stays variable. Note generation itself is not deterministic across reruns, which is why the committed file, not the script, is the source of truth.
build_effort: About 1-1.5 days for an agent here: batch script with JSON schema and quote check (~0.5 day), a 40-family pilot and eyeballing (~2 hours), data file plus compactCatalog change and a test that every `evidence` string is a substring of its source (~0.5 day). Existing patterns to copy: askClaudeCode and RESULT_SCHEMA in server/vibe.ts, the cached source folders under server/.cache.
per_search_cost_and_latency: Zero extra calls if notes sit in the cached prompt (cost is the extra input tokens above; on `claude -p` a quota use, not dollars). If used only for a shortlist, it is cheaper than today because the main prompt shrinks.
one_off_cost: Batch labelling of 1,507 rows (measured sizes: ~232k tokens of Google text, ~19k of Fontshare text, plus ~40k of instructions across ~60-70 calls, ~105k tokens out). At list prices on the pricing page (2026-10-03): Haiku 4.5 ($1 in / $5 out per MTok) about $0.8, with the Batch API half of that; Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10) about $1.6 (newer tokenizer, ~30% more tokens). On the subscription through `claude -p`, about 60-70 calls, perhaps 15-40 minutes [uncertain: not timed]. Downloads: none (descriptions already in the scratch folder, Fontshare in fontshare.json).
human_effort: About 1-2 hours first time: read the 40-family pilot, then spot-check 5% of the output (~75 notes) and the 100 shortest or empty ones. As the catalog grows: a glance at new notes per refresh (a few minutes).
asset_access: Google texts are on disk (SCRATCH/gf, 1,754 files). To refresh without cloning the repo (the API reports 3.3 GB): list DESCRIPTION paths with the Git trees API and fetch each from raw.githubusercontent.com (about 1,750 tiny requests, 0.2-0.3 s apart), or use a sparse, blobless clone. Fontshare: the story arrives in the call the catalog build already makes. Indie: nothing to fetch for prose; Velvetyne only through GitLab as the app already does, never velvetyne.fr.
licence_and_provenance: Google: the README says top-level directories indicate the licence of all files in them, so a description under ofl/ falls under the same folder licence as its font (OFL 1.1; apache/ Apache 2; ufl/ Ubuntu Font Licence) [uncertain: whether prose counts as 'font software or documentation' under the OFL]. Fontshare: the fonts are under the ITF Free Font License; the story text has no stated licence [uncertain]. The condensed notes are short factual paraphrases with a quoted span; the app also exports a static online build (export-static.ts), so publishing the notes there should keep the quote short, credit the source and avoid long copies. Not legal advice.
etiquette: No new requests are needed for a first run (all text is already on disk). A refresh is about 1,750 tiny raw.githubusercontent.com fetches at a polite pace plus one Fontshare API call. No robots or bot-protection issue; never velvetyne.fr (nothing here needs it).
maintenance_and_freshness: Texts change slowly (some carry update notes from 2015-2023). The catalog grows: 256 Google families in today's catalog were added in 2024 or later, 202 true Google families have no description in my copy, and each new family needs one new note. With a stored source hash a rerun costs only the new or changed rows (a few cents). Fontshare adds few families.
risks_and_limitations: (1) Coverage: 71.8% of rows; none for the 275 indie rows, where the gap is. (2) Content: 18% of texts have no look word and many are history or language notes. (3) The LLM step can invent looks; mitigated by a required quote that is string-checked, but a quote can still be misread. (4) Notes in the prompt double its size if applied to all rows, and the model may over-weight literal words ('speedy script' beats a better-fitting sans). (5) Tag and text can disagree (Racing Sans One: tag says Active, text says nothing about speed; Kaushan Script's text is about keeping energy in the letters and its tag is Active 89, they agree). (6) Licence of the prose is unclear for the public static build. (7) My keyword counts are rough regex counts, and my 17-font oracle is small and built from the same texts.
evaluation_hook: Pilot of 40 descriptions (my 17 oracle fonts, Exo 2, Saira, Teko, and 20 random): check every quote is a substring, read the notes, and mark each as faithful or not. Then run 20-30 mood and motion queries with and without notes for the thin-tag rows and have a person rate the result grids; target is more correct picks among rows with two tags or fewer. Held-out check: hide Google's Futuristic/Techno tags and see whether the note's tech score recovers them (expect 12 of 15 explicit cases).
recommendation_for_font_explorer: USE PARTLY, as a cheap second signal and not as the main fix. Generate notes once for all 1,507 rows that have prose (about $1 or a short `claude -p` run), keep a quoted evidence span for each, but put notes in the prompt only for the roughly 570 rows with fewer than three tags, and use the motion/tech scores for a pre-filter. Do not stuff notes into every row. Why: they fix exactly the kind of gap the brief names (Exo 2, Oxanium, Rajdhani, Contrail One, Smooch, Hurricane, Reggae One, Tourney, Goldman get a motion or tech reading they lack today) and they explain themselves with the designer's own sentence. They do not reach the 275 indie rows or the 115 non-Google Fontsource rows without text; for those, measured traits, a vision pass or tag transfer are the real answer. Position relative to the other items: after the near-free Google-tag changes (keep scores, fix renamed families), alongside measured slant and width, before any vision-model run. SMALLEST FIRST STEP: pilot 40 families (my oracle fonts plus Exo 2, Saira, Teko and 20 random) through Haiku with a JSON schema {looks, evidence, motion 0-3, tech 0-3}, check the quotes by substring, read the output, then run the other 1,467. About half a day to the pilot verdict.
